title: The Greatest Work of Western Philosophy
author: The Culturist
summary: The Culturist makes the case that Plato's Republic is essential reading because it frames the perennial questions at the root of Western thought and exposes the unexamined assumptions of modern readers. The piece opens with the claim that Western philosophy is a footnote to Plato and traces the Republic's influence from Aristotle and Augustine to 1984 and The Matrix. It argues that the dialogue's refusal to neatly resolve questions about justice, legitimacy, rule, and education trains readers to locate the core disagreements beneath contemporary political debates. A second section connects Plato to Christianity through the 'fullness of time' convergence of Jerusalem, Rome, and Athens, noting which Platonic ideas the Church retained and which it rejected. The final argument is that reading Plato, precisely because he is so un-modern, lets readers see their own culture's presuppositions the way a fish might finally notice water. The essay then announces a year-long Republic read-along from its sister publication, but its core claim is a Great Books argument about what a formative education should include.
points: The Republic's lasting power lies in the foundational questions it poses about justice, legitimacy, who should rule, and the purpose of education, rather than in tidy answers.
Because Plato leaves questions unresolved, readers learn to identify the underlying conceptual disputes, such as competing ideas of justice, beneath modern political fights.
The essay situates Plato inside the Jerusalem-Rome-Athens synthesis, noting the Church kept ideas like the immaterial soul while discarding eugenics and transmigration of souls.
Reading an 'un-modern' thinker is presented as a way to escape the cave of modern presuppositions about democracy, equality, and freedom.
The piece positions a slow, scholar-guided read-along as the right way to approach a text that is transformative but difficult.
quotes: The Republic is Plato’s most famous work of philosophy, and by far the most impactful. Imagined as a conversation between his mentor Socrates and various members of Athenian society, the Republic has influenced everyone from Aristotle to Augustine, Mussolini to MLK.

Whether you know it or not, you swim in the ideas contained in the Republic. From the Allegory of the Cave (which influenced everything from 1984 to The Matrix) to more complex ideas like those of justice, political legitimacy, and the tripartite soul, Plato tills the soil from which the Western intellectual tradition springs.
What is justice? Why should I be good when injustice benefits me? What makes a political regime legitimate? Who should rule? What is the purpose of education?

If you’re new to philosophy, this might feel frustrating. But the benefit of this approach is that it helps you identify the main struggles at the heart of any contemporary debate or political faultline.

Traditionally, the fullness of time has been understood as the historical moment in which Hebrew faith coincided with Roman order and Greek reason. The inheritance of Jerusalem, Rome, and Athens sits not just at the heart of Western Civilization, but at the very core of Christianity itself.

Of course, not all of Plato was accepted by the Church — while concepts like the immaterial soul and the insufficiency of earthly pleasure were retained, others like eugenics and the transmigration of souls were cast aside.
Just as a fish can’t recognize the water it swims in, we as modern individuals can’t recognize our own assumptions about the world. Plato helps remedy that.
Many readers of Plato are shocked to discover just how un-modern he is, yet at the same time find a sense of freedom in this revelation.
